sections.h2: Where does a deed go in Marion County, Ohio?
sections.html:
A Marion County deed passes through three offices in a fixed order: the County Engineer, the County Auditor and the County Recorder. The recorder is the last stop and the one that makes the deed part of the public record. The recorder's number is 740-223-4100, the auditor's is 740-223-4020 and the engineer's is 740-223-4110.

The recorder also keeps mortgages, easements and other land documents for every parcel in the county. Its online records system lets anyone search property records, but copies and certified copies need an in-person visit or a written request with payment enclosed. The system carries a disclaimer: users must check the actual document, because the database can change without notice.

sections.h2: What happens at each of the three offices?
sections.html:
The county's own pages describe the sequence in detail, and it differs from counties where the auditor goes first.

  • Engineer. Staff compare the legal description on the deed with their records and stamp it approved. The stamp is good for 60 days, so a deed that sits past that date has to be stamped again.
  • Auditor. A conveyance form is completed and signed, the fee is paid before anything is processed, and the auditor stamps the deed as transferred.
  • Recorder. Staff check that the deed was executed correctly and that both stamps are present, then record it. The original is held for imaging and data entry and is later mailed or picked up.

The same route applies to a certificate of transfer, an affidavit of survivor, a life estate, a transfer on death designation or a land contract. Because the engineer approves the legal description before money changes hands, mistakes in an old description tend to surface early.

sections.h2: What does it cost to transfer and record a deed in Marion County?
sections.html:
Two sets of charges apply, one at the auditor and one at the recorder. The auditor's conveyance fee is set locally, and the recorder's fee comes from state law. A county notice on the recorder's home page says Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to recording fees for most documents beginning January 1, 2025.

Marion County deed charges as printed on the county's own pages
OfficeCharge as stated
EngineerLegal description stamp, valid for 60 days
Auditor, conveyance fee$4.00 for every $1,000 of sale price
Auditor, line fee$0.50 for each parcel in the transfer
Auditor, small saleMinimum conveyance fee of $4.00 plus line fees when the price is under $1,000
Recorder, base fee$34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after (rate listed as of October 17, 2019)

The auditor's transfer fee calculator, which the county posts online, asks for the total sale price rounded up to the next dollar and the number of parcels. A transfer with no sale price can qualify for an exemption on the state form DTE 100 EX. Exempt transfers still pay the line fee, so ask the auditor for the exact total before you write the check.

sections.h2: Can a Marion County deed be mailed in?
sections.html:
Yes, but only in the right order. The recorder's page says no deed is accepted by mail unless it already carries current engineer and auditor stamps, a rule in place since September 1, 2005. The county lays out the mailing steps as follows:

  • Mail only the deed to the engineer, with a self-addressed stamped envelope for its return
  • Send the stamped deed to the auditor with a signed conveyance form, a check for the fee and another return envelope
  • Send the twice-stamped deed to the recorder with a check for the recording fee

Turnaround at the recorder is about five days. That time covers proofing, imaging and a comparison of the image against the original before it is returned in the envelope you supplied. Anyone who prefers to skip the mail can use an electronic filing company. The recorder lists CSC at 855-200-1150, ePN at 888-325-3365, Simplifile at 800-460-5657 and Indecomm at 651-765-6400.

sections.h2: Does the recorder's calendar affect a closing date?
sections.html:
It can. The recorder posts closures for the year, and they go beyond the usual federal holidays. For 2026 the list included Good Friday, Juneteenth, a half day plus a full day around Independence Day, and a Thursday afternoon and Friday in September for the Popcorn Festival because of parking problems downtown. The same list shows closures on Veterans Day, the day before and two days after Thanksgiving, Friday afternoon on December 11, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, and New Year's Day 2027.

A closing set for a closure day cannot be recorded until the office reopens. Ask the title company which day it plans to file. Recording after the funds move is normal, but a seller who needs proof of recording before handing over keys should say so early.

sections.h2: What is Marion County like for a home sale?
sections.html:
Marion County sits in central Ohio with Crawford, Morrow, Delaware, Union, Hardin and Wyandot counties around it. The state erected it on February 20, 1820 and reorganized it in 1824, naming it for Revolutionary War officer Francis Marion. At 404 square miles it is the fifth-smallest county in Ohio, and the city of Marion is both seat and largest city. U.S. 23 and a web of state routes, including 4, 37, 95 and 309, run through it.

Census figures give a sense of the housing stock:

  • Population: 65,359 in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 65,115
  • Homes occupied by their owners: 67.5 percent
  • Midpoint value of an owned home, 2020 to 2024: $156,800
  • Midpoint gross rent: $864
  • Household income at the midpoint: $59,371

The 2020 census counted 27,348 housing units, 8.8 percent of them vacant, and 65.3 percent of residents lived in urban areas. Builders pulled 60 permits in 2025, so most sales involve existing houses.

sections.h2: What should a seller do about taxes before the deed is filed?
sections.html:
Contact the County Treasurer at 740-223-4030, since that office receives all property tax payments. The county auditor explains that tax rates come from voter-approved levies and that Ohio caps unvoted taxation at 10 mills, or $10 per $1,000 of assessed value. Anything above that was approved by county voters.

Payment can be made through the auditor's property search site. The county adds a 2.5 percent processing fee, with a $1.50 minimum, to debit and credit cards, and a flat $1.50 to e-check payments up to $10,000, and it shows the fee before you submit. A delinquent land tax notice for 2026 set September 18 as the date to pay in the treasurer's office. Marion County sellers should ask for a payoff figure early, because any balance has to be settled from the proceeds so the buyer receives a clear title.

faqs.q: What phone number do I call for the Marion County Recorder?
faqs.a: 740-223-4100. The county's engineer is at 740-223-4110 and the auditor at 740-223-4020.

faqs.q: How long is the engineer's stamp good for?
faqs.a: Sixty days. After that, the deed must be stamped again before the auditor and recorder will accept it.

faqs.q: What is the Marion County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price plus 50 cents for each parcel. Non-exempt sales under $1,000 pay a $4.00 minimum plus line fees.

faqs.q: How long does the recorder take to return a deed?
faqs.a: About five days, according to the county's mail instructions. The time covers proofing, imaging and comparing the image with the original.

faqs.q: Can I e-file a deed in Marion County?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder lists four e-filing companies: CSC, ePN, Simplifile and Indecomm. Contact one of them for setup.
